record.paper_title: Open Questions in Massive Star Research across Cosmic Scales
record.original_question: How can resolved observations of individual massive stars and clusters be connected to integrated-light observations so that population synthesis correctly maps detailed stellar physics into galaxy-scale predictions? The answer requires determining what multi-epoch spectroscopy, ultraviolet diagnostics, and future facilities such as the Extremely Large Telescope and the Habitable Worlds Observatory must measure to close remaining knowledge gaps in massive-star multiplicity, binary-interaction outcomes, stellar feedback, and integrated population modeling.

evidence.quote: Spectroscopic observations, ideally multi-epoch, are the key to get proper answers, in particular as multiplicity is almost everywhere, but aquiring this data for large samples remains an ongoing challenge. The UV marks a particularly crucial regime here as it bears unique diagnostics for many decisive outcomes of binary interaction.

Connecting resolved and integrated observations of massive stars is challenging, but essential for a coherent understanding of massive stars and to ensure population synthesis correctly maps the insights from resolved populations. This is particularly crucial as many regimes will remain limited to integrated-light studies.

To close knowledge gaps, forthcoming facilities such the ELT or eventually the Habitable World Observatory can become gamechangers, but need to be designed with massive stars in mind to provide the necessary senstivitiy and diagnostics.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider populations of massive stars (initial masses ≳ 8 M_sun), which can be studied in two complementary ways: (i) resolved observations, in which individual stars and star clusters are spatially and spectrally distinguished, yielding stellar parameters such as effective temperatures, luminosities, surface abundances, mass-loss rates, rotation rates, multiplicity status, and orbital parameters of binaries; and (ii) integrated-light observations, in which only the spatially unresolved combined spectrum of an entire stellar population (e.g., a distant galaxy or H II region) is available, characterized by integrated spectral energy distributions, emission and absorption line strengths, and ultraviolet (UV) continuum and wind features. Population synthesis is the modeling framework that takes as input distributions of stellar physics ingredients—initial mass function, binary fraction and orbital parameter distributions, prescriptions for stellar evolution including binary interaction (mass transfer, common envelope, mergers), stellar winds, and feedback (ionizing photon production, mechanical and radiative feedback)—and outputs predicted integrated-light observables for stellar populations of given age and metallicity.

Formulate and solve the following problem. Specify a concrete observational and modeling program that establishes a quantitative mapping from resolved stellar measurements to integrated-light predictions such that population synthesis faithfully reproduces galaxy-scale observables. In particular:

(a) Identify the minimal set of multi-epoch spectroscopic measurements (cadence, signal-to-noise, wavelength coverage, sample size as a function of metallicity) required to determine the intrinsic distributions of massive-star multiplicity properties (binary fraction, mass-ratio and period distributions) at metallicities ranging from near-solar down to those representative of the early universe.

(b) Specify which UV diagnostics (e.g., resonance wind lines, photospheric features, nebular continuum) are necessary and sufficient to constrain the outcomes of binary interaction (stripped stars, mergers, accretors, post-common-envelope systems) and their feedback contributions, and quantify the precision needed for these diagnostics to discriminate among competing binary-evolution prescriptions.

(c) Derive the sensitivity, spatial resolution, and spectral resolution requirements that future facilities of the class of a 30–40 m ground-based Extremely Large Telescope and a UV/optical/IR space-based Habitable Worlds Observatory must meet to acquire (a) and (b) for representative samples across cosmic environments.

(d) Construct an explicit prescription by which the resulting resolved-population constraints are propagated into population synthesis models so that integrated-light predictions—ionizing photon production, mechanical feedback energetics, UV spectral morphology, and chemical yields—agree with observations of unresolved stellar populations to within stated tolerances.

Provide either a constructive solution or a rigorous demonstration that such a program is sufficient to close the present knowledge gaps in massive-star multiplicity, binary-interaction outcomes, stellar feedback, and integrated population modeling.
artifact.status_search_result: This is an active, open research program in massive-star astrophysics. Connecting resolved and integrated-light observations through population synthesis remains an unsolved challenge highlighted in recent reviews, with major future facilities (ELT, HWO) still in design/planning stages and ongoing surveys (e.g., BLOeM, XShootU, ULLYSES) only beginning to deliver the requisite multi-epoch and UV data. No comprehensive solution exists in the current literature.

status_evidence.title: ULLYSES: A Hubble UV Legacy Library
status_evidence.snippet: Director's Discretionary program providing UV spectroscopic templates of massive stars at low metallicity to support population synthesis.
status_evidence.claim: Foundational UV diagnostic data for massive-star population synthesis are still being assembled, indicating the problem is open.

status_evidence.title: Habitable Worlds Observatory
status_evidence.snippet: NASA's next flagship UV/optical/IR space telescope, currently in pre-formulation.
status_evidence.claim: HWO is still in early design, so the proposed program cannot yet be executed.
